---
title: "Raise a regulatory dragon: FDA statistics guidance"
description: >
  Four public FDA guidances that every trial statistician knows, read,
  questioned, and used to fine-tune a 3B model on an 8 GB laptop.
---

<img class="df-post-mascot" src="../dragon.svg" alt="The dragonfarm dragon: a minimal orange dragon head in profile, with amber horns and neck spikes">

<p class="lead">If you work in clinical trials, you know these documents by heart, or wish you did: FDA's guidances on covariate adjustment and multiple endpoints, the ICH E9(R1) addendum on estimands, and FDA's one-page statement on statistical software. We gave all four to dragonfarm on an 8 GB laptop, asked them questions, and trained a model on them. Here is what happened, numbers and all.</p>

## The documents

Four public guidances, 65 pages, downloaded from fda.gov:

| Guidance | Year | Pages | Chunks |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials](https://www.fda.gov/media/148910/download) | 2023 | 12 | 29 |
| [Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials](https://www.fda.gov/media/162416/download) | 2022 | 29 | 54 |
| [E9(R1) Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis](https://www.fda.gov/media/148473/download) | 2021 | 23 | 72 |
| [Statistical Software Clarifying Statement](https://www.fda.gov/media/109552/download) | 2015 | 1 | 2 |

Reading and indexing all four took under a minute.

## Before any training, it already knows them

RAG is built in, so the first thing you can do is ask. We wrote 24
questions with answers checked against the guidances, and 8 the
guidances don't cover. Both an untrained 3B and an untrained 7B got
**all 24 right** and declined **all 8**.

<div class="df-ba df-qa">
<div class="df-reply after"><span class="df-who">Question</span><p class="df-q">In the hypothetical example in Table 1 of the covariate guidance, what is the unconditional odds ratio?</p><p>In the hypothetical example presented in Table 1 of the covariate guidance document, the unconditional odds ratio in the target population is 4.8. This value represents the overall effect of the treatment across the entire population, as opposed to the conditional odds ratios observed within biomarker-positive and biomarker-negative subgroups, which were found to be 8.0 in both subgroups.</p><span class="df-note">Qwen 2.5 7B, untrained, 11 seconds</span></div>
<div class="df-reply after"><span class="df-who">Question</span><p class="df-q">Does FDA require sponsors to use a specific statistical software package?</p><p>No, the FDA does not require sponsors to use a specific statistical software package. [...] However, the FDA does expect sponsors to fully document the software package(s) used for statistical analyses, including the version and build identification, and to consult with FDA statisticians regarding the choice and suitability of statistical software packages at an early stage in the product development process.</p><span class="df-note">Qwen 2.5 7B, untrained. Good news for R users.</span></div>
</div>

Asked for the half-life of adalimumab, it said the documents focus on
statistical methods and don't cover it. Good dragon.

## It writes its own practice questions

Next, dragonfarm read every chunk and wrote practice questions with
answers: **459 in 19 minutes, 407 kept** by its filters. A few of them:

- *What is a potential benefit of using a composite endpoint?* A composite
  endpoint can provide a substantially higher overall event rate, allowing
  a study with a reasonable sample size and duration to have adequate
  statistical power.
- *What types of outcomes can covariate-adjusted estimators of unconditional
  treatment effects be applied to?* Binary, ordinal, count, and
  time-to-event outcomes.
- *How should secondary trial objectives be handled in terms of
  estimands?* Those likely to support regulatory decisions should have
  their own explicitly specified estimands, each with a main estimator and
  a suitable sensitivity analysis.

We checked 15 kept questions by hand. Thirteen were accurate and useful.
Two show why the review step exists: one overstated the guidance ("a
single primary endpoint is *needed* to avoid multiplicity issues"; the
guidance also allows co-primary and composite endpoints), and one was
trivia from the reference list (the title of *Multiple Comparisons Using
R*, a fine book, but not a lesson). In the app you would untick those two.

## Then it trains, on the laptop

A 3B model in 4-bit trained on the 407 questions plus 61 "not covered"
examples in **28 minutes** on an 8 GB laptop GPU, with Unsloth, which
dragonfarm now uses on NVIDIA GPUs. The standard trainer took 41 minutes
on the same rows; the table below is from that run, and the Unsloth-trained
model scored the same (23 of 24 right, 8 of 8 declined).

| Model | Right, of 24 | Declined, of 8 | Median answer | Median time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3B, before training | 24 | 8 | 61 words | 9.2 s |
| 3B, after training | 23 | 8 | 16 words | 6.6 s |
| 7B, no training | 24 | 8 | 64 words | 10.9 s |

The trained dragon knows nothing it didn't know before: RAG already
supplied the facts. What changed is its voice. It now answers the way the
practice answers were written: one direct sentence, four times shorter and
a third faster.

A smaller dragon is a different story. The 1.5B got 19 of 24 right and
declined 7 of 8 before training; trained on the same kind of questions, it
got 22 or 23 right and declined all 8 (two runs with different seeds). So
train a small model to make it better, and a 3B or 7B to make it yours.

<div class="df-ba df-qa">
<div class="df-reply"><span class="df-who">Before training</span><p class="df-q">Which strategy restricts the observation time to before the intercurrent event?</p><p>The while-on-treatment strategy restricts the observation time to before the intercurrent event. This is evident from [1], which states "While-on-Treatment Strategies: Like the composite variable strategy, the while-on-treatment strategy can hence be thought of as having an impact on the definition of the variable, in this case, by restricting the observation time of interest to the time before the intercurrent event."</p></div>
<div class="df-reply after"><span class="df-who">After training</span><p class="df-q">Which strategy restricts the observation time to before the intercurrent event?</p><p>The while-on-treatment strategy restricts the observation time to before the intercurrent event. [1]</p></div>
</div>

One cost: the trained model declined one question it should have
answered (other names for the g-computation estimator). Training with
"not covered" examples makes a model cautious; usually that is the right
direction, and here it was once too cautious.

## Teach it a house style

Say your team wants every answer in two lines: the answer, then the
guidance it comes from. You can ask for that in a prompt, or train it in.
We tried both on the same 3B and the same 32 questions.

| | Asked for in a prompt | Trained in |
|---|---|---|
| Two-line format | 30 of 32 | 32 of 32 |
| Right guidance named | 13 of 32 | 29 of 32 |
| Right answers | 19 of 24 | 22 of 24 |

Asked in a prompt, the untrained dragon often named the file instead of the
guidance ("fda-covariate-adjustment-2023.pdf") and, tangled in the
instructions, declined five questions it could answer. Trained for 42
minutes on 422 practice answers written in the house style, it used the
style every time without being told:

<div class="df-ba df-qa">
<div class="df-reply after"><span class="df-who">Trained in, no instructions</span><p class="df-q">In the hypothetical example in Table 1 of the covariate guidance, what is the unconditional odds ratio?</p><p>Answer: The unconditional odds ratio in the hypothetical target population is 4.8. [1]<br>Guidance: Adjusting for Covariates in Randomized Clinical Trials (FDA, 2023)</p></div>
<div class="df-reply after"><span class="df-who">Trained in, no instructions</span><p class="df-q">What is the PDUFA application fee for fiscal year 2025?</p><p>Answer: The documents do not cover this.<br>Guidance: none</p></div>
</div>

This is where fine-tuning earns its keep: not new facts, but a habit.

## What this tells you

- **For facts, start with RAG.** On clean regulatory text, retrieval plus
  an untrained model was already perfect on our questions.
- **Fine-tune for voice.** Training is how you get a model that answers
  the way your team writes: short and direct, a fixed template, your
  terminology. For a fixed format it beat prompting on every count, and it
  also makes a small model faster.
- **Review the practice questions.** Two of fifteen needed unticking. The
  review takes minutes and decides what the model learns.

These are our questions on four documents, not a validation. Guidance is
non-binding, and nothing here is regulatory advice: check the guidance
itself before you rely on an answer.

## Try it yourself

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dragonfarm)
pdfs <- c("fda-covariate-adjustment-2023.pdf",
          "fda-multiple-endpoints-2022.pdf",
          "ich-e9r1-estimands-2021.pdf",
          "fda-statistical-software-statement-2015.pdf")
docs <- dragon_documents(pdfs, name = "fda-stats")
dragon_ask(docs, "Which standard error does FDA suggest?")

qa <- dragon_questions(docs)   # review them in dragon_app()
dragon_questions_save(qa)
run <- dragon_train(
  dragon_questions_dataset(qa, docs),
  "Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct",
  hardware = dragon_hardware(load_in_4bit = TRUE),
  args = dragon_train_args(batch_size = 1, grad_accum = 16,
                           gradient_checkpointing = TRUE,
                           max_seq_len = 1536),
  wait = TRUE
)
```

Or open `dragon_app()`, drop the four PDFs on the Documents step, and
follow the steps. Measured on an RTX 4060 laptop GPU with 8 GB, dragonfarm
0.4.0, on 16 October 2026.
